headline: High-risk shared-write and shared-state pair: Flowise can write shared files while semantica has broader mutable data/tool access, creating dangerous conflict and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write server filesystem and uploaded files, while semantica can ingest local files, web pages, and MCP resources. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if one agent’s outputs are placed in shared files or resources. No direct parser-hijack evidence is provided, so I rate it medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Flowise writes agent-generated text into a shared file or uploaded artifact that semantica later ingests
IF semantica treats file or MCP resource content as instruction-bearing text without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories
Disable automatic ingestion of shared artifacts
Add provenance labels to all exchanged files
Require a human review step before semantica consumes Flowise outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and model provider keys, and semantica handles enterprise data, contracts, decision records, and secrets. Both have filesystem access, and semantica also has MCP/API surfaces that can move data outward. In default shared-workspace deployments, sensitive Flowise artifacts can be exposed to semantica and then propagated further.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace or datastore
IF Flowise artifacts include provider keys, tool credentials, or chatflow inputs
IF semantica exports ingested enterprise data through its API/MCP/CLI surfaces
mitigations: Put each agent in a separate workspace
Redact secrets before any file handoff
Restrict semantica egress to a test endpoint
Rotate any credentials that may have been exposed
Log and review all cross-agent file transfers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, read files, and use networked tools; Flowise also has broad egress while semantica can modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. With shared-state semantics on both sides, concurrent writes to the same resources can corrupt files, graphs, or repositories unless explicit locking exists, which is not documented here.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, repository, or datastore
IF concurrent runs occur without external locking
IF semantica writes git or graph state while Flowise writes flow artifacts
mitigations: Assign disjoint write paths
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent runs during shared updates
Snapshot state before each run
Use separate git branches or repositories

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise is a graph-based orchestration layer whose outputs can become downstream inputs, while semantica is designed for deterministic graph construction and provenance but still consumes external files and APIs. If semantica treats Flowise-produced content as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into stored decision records or graph state without verification.
conditions: IF semantica ingests Flowise-generated text, facts, or citations as trusted input
IF no verification or provenance gate is inserted between them
IF downstream actions or records are created from that ingested content
mitigations: Insert a verification step between agents
Require provenance metadata on every transferred artifact
Block automatic promotion of unreviewed outputs
Compare outputs against source documents before storage
Limit semantica to read-only consumption of Flowise results

E_compliance.rationale: Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and secrets, while semantica handles enterprise data, contracts, audit trails, and private keys. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so I cannot claim a concrete breach; however, the mismatch in data classes and retention-sensitive artifacts makes compliance drift plausible if the pair shares regulated content.
conditions: IF regulated data such as contracts, audit trails, or secrets is routed through both agents
IF one agent’s logging or retention policy is broader than the other’s
IF residency or certification requirements apply to the shared data class
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents
Disable logging of sensitive fields
Keep regulated data out of shared flows
Document retention and deletion rules for both systems
Run a quick compliance review on the exact data classes in scope
